Name: Sarah Apple
Badge: Teacher as Researcher: Cultivating Literacy Routines
Looking back on this inquiry cycle, what did you learn about your teaching and your students that you might not have noticed otherwise? How did engaging in this teacher-research process shape or shift your thinking about your classroom practice?:

It is so easy to get caught in the whirlwind of the pacing guide and the race to the common assessments. You know - the things that spark ZERO joy. It was very refreshing, as always with the writing project, to just step back and look at things through a fresh lens. It's great to get some new strategies to try or reminders of strategies you may have forgotten about - and the challenge/accountability to put them into practice. It's good for both me and my students to try new things. My students were also tickled that I was taking a class and wanted pictures of their work to share. And some of their responses - though simple and on a serious topic - can be funny. "Vaping can kill you in a peach mango way." I'm not sure if they intended that to be funny or not but it did amuse me.

Share one artifact or anecdote from trying out your chosen strategy (e.g., a piece of student work, notes from your Writer’s Notebook, a classroom snapshot, or a brief story from the experience).:
What new questions or next steps are you leaving this module with? How might you continue to explore or build on this inquiry in your future teaching?:

I want to try They Say/I Say in a multimodal way with an article that has images/graphs/etc. I would like them to put this into practice both with excerpts from the text that they annotated (or that I specify) but also any images that accompany the article. Especially in science, the imagery that goes with texts can be very important and add deeper meaning. I would like to use They Say/I Say as a way to scaffold and structure that meaning making.
